thinkers.name: Thales of Miletus
thinkers.bio: Thales is traditionally counted as the first Greek philosopher and one of the Seven Sages. He sought a natural rather than mythological explanation of the world, proposing water as the origin of all things. Later tradition credits him with geometric theorems and with predicting a solar eclipse in 585 BCE. No writings by him survive; we know him through Aristotle and later reports.
thinkers.start: Aristotle, Metaphysics Book I (his account of the early thinkers)

thinkers.name: Anaximander
thinkers.bio: A pupil or associate of Thales, Anaximander proposed that the origin of things is the apeiron, the boundless or indefinite. He produced one of the first maps of the known world and a model of the Earth floating unsupported at the centre of the cosmos. A single sentence of his is the oldest surviving fragment of Western philosophy.

books.title: On Nature (fragment)
books.note: The oldest surviving fragment of Greek philosophy.

thinkers.start: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Anaximenes
thinkers.bio: The third Milesian, Anaximenes held that air is the underlying substance of everything. Air becomes fire when rarefied and wind, cloud, water, earth and stone as it condenses. This gave a mechanism of change rather than just a first stuff.
thinkers.start: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Pythagoras
thinkers.bio: Pythagoras founded a religious and philosophical community at Croton in southern Italy. His followers taught the transmigration of souls, a disciplined way of life and the idea that number and harmony underlie the cosmos. Because the school attributed its discoveries to the master, it is hard to separate his own views from those of later Pythagoreans.
ideas: Number as the principle of things
Philosophy as a way of life
thinkers.quote: All things are number.
thinkers.start: Charles Kahn, Pythagoras and the Pythagoreans

thinkers.name: Xenophanes
thinkers.bio: A wandering poet-philosopher, Xenophanes attacked the anthropomorphic gods of Homer and Hesiod. He argued for a single god unlike mortals in body or thought. He also raised early doubts about whether humans can attain certain knowledge.
thinkers.start: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Heraclitus
thinkers.bio: Heraclitus of Ephesus wrote in deliberately obscure aphorisms, earning the name "the Obscure". He taught that the world is an ever-living fire, constantly changing yet governed by a rational order, the logos. Opposites are bound together in tension, and strife is the father of all.

books.title: Fragments
books.note: Aphorisms on flux, fire and the unity of opposites.

thinkers.quote: You could not step twice into the same river.
thinkers.start: Charles Kahn, The Art and Thought of Heraclitus

thinkers.name: Parmenides
thinkers.bio: Parmenides of Elea wrote a philosophical poem in which a goddess reveals the Way of Truth and the Way of Opinion. He argued that what is cannot not be, so coming-to-be, change and plurality are impossible. His argument set the agenda for Plato, the atomists and much of later metaphysics.

books.title: On Nature (poem)
books.note: The Way of Truth versus the Way of Opinion.

thinkers.quote: What is, is, and what is not, is not.
thinkers.start: Plato, Parmenides; then the poem itself (Gallop translation)

thinkers.name: Zeno of Elea
thinkers.bio: Zeno was the student of Parmenides and defended him with paradoxes. His arguments, like Achilles and the tortoise and the arrow, aim to show that motion and plurality lead to contradiction. Aristotle called him the inventor of dialectic.

thinkers.name: Empedocles
thinkers.bio: Empedocles proposed four roots, earth, water, air and fire, mixed and separated by two forces, Love and Strife. The cosmos cycles between total unity and total separation. He was also a poet, physician and reputed wonder-worker.
ideas: Love and Strife as cosmic forces

books.title: On Nature
books.note: Physical poem on the four roots.

books.title: Purifications
books.note: Religious poem on the soul's exile.

thinkers.start: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Anaxagoras
thinkers.bio: Anaxagoras brought philosophy to Athens, where he was a friend of Pericles. He held that everything contains a portion of everything and that Nous, Mind, set the cosmos in motion. He was charged with impiety for calling the sun a fiery stone and left Athens.
ideas: "In everything there is a portion of everything"

thinkers.name: Democritus
thinkers.bio: Democritus developed, with his teacher Leucippus, the theory that reality consists of indivisible atoms moving in the void. Qualities like colour and taste exist by convention, not in the atoms. Known as the "laughing philosopher", he also wrote on ethics, recommending cheerfulness.
thinkers.start: Kirk, Raven & Schofield, The Presocratic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Protagoras
thinkers.bio: Protagoras was the most famous of the Sophists, paid teachers of rhetoric and virtue. His claim that man is the measure of all things became the classic statement of relativism. Plato wrote a dialogue named after him.
ideas: Man is the measure of all things

thinkers.name: Socrates
thinkers.bio: Socrates wrote nothing; we know him from Plato, Xenophon and Aristophanes. He questioned Athenians about virtue and showed their claims to knowledge were unfounded, professing his own ignorance. He was tried for impiety and corrupting the youth and was executed by hemlock.
thinkers.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living for a human being.

thinkers.name: Diogenes of Sinope
thinkers.bio: Diogenes lived in a large jar in Athens and scorned convention, wealth and social status. He taught by provocative example that virtue requires living according to nature. Anecdotes of him and Alexander the Great became famous; he left no surviving writings.
thinkers.start: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Eminent Philosophers, Book VI

thinkers.name: Plato
thinkers.bio: Plato was a student of Socrates and founded the Academy in Athens. His dialogues, mostly featuring Socrates, cover ethics, politics, knowledge, love and the soul. He argued that the visible world imitates eternal Forms grasped by reason. Whitehead called European philosophy a series of footnotes to Plato.

books.title: Symposium
books.note: Speeches on love ascending to Beauty itself.

books.title: Republic
books.note: Justice, the ideal city and the Cave.

books.title: Phaedo
books.note: The immortality of the soul and Socrates' death.

books.title: Laws
books.note: Plato's last and longest work, a practical constitution.

thinkers.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living.

thinkers.name: Aristotle
thinkers.bio: Aristotle studied at Plato's Academy for twenty years, tutored Alexander the Great and founded the Lyceum. He wrote on logic, physics, biology, ethics, politics, rhetoric and poetics, founding several of those fields. He rejected separate Forms and located form in individual substances.
ideas: Virtue as a mean, happiness as flourishing

books.title: Metaphysics
books.note: Being qua being, substance, the unmoved mover.

thinkers.quote: All men by nature desire to know.

thinkers.name: Epicurus
thinkers.bio: Epicurus founded the Garden in Athens. He taught that pleasure, understood as freedom from bodily pain and mental disturbance, is the goal of life. Drawing on Democritus' atomism, he argued that death is nothing to us and that the gods do not intervene in the world.
thinkers.quote: Death is nothing to us.

thinkers.name: Pyrrho
thinkers.bio: Pyrrho travelled with Alexander's army to India and returned teaching that things are indeterminable. The right response is to suspend judgment, which brings tranquillity. He wrote nothing, and later Pyrrhonism took his name.

thinkers.name: Zeno of Citium
thinkers.bio: Zeno founded Stoicism, teaching at the Painted Porch (Stoa Poikile) in Athens. He taught that virtue is the only good and that the wise live in agreement with nature and reason. His works are lost, but his system was developed by Cleanthes and Chrysippus.
thinkers.quote: Happiness is a good flow of life.

thinkers.name: Chrysippus
thinkers.bio: Chrysippus was the third head of the Stoa and its greatest systematizer. He developed Stoic propositional logic and its theories of fate and causation. Ancient writers said that without Chrysippus there would have been no Stoa.
thinkers.start: A. A. Long & D. N. Sedley, The Hellenistic Philosophers

thinkers.name: Cicero
thinkers.bio: Cicero was a Roman statesman, orator and lawyer who brought Greek philosophy into Latin. He wrote on the state, law, duty, the gods and the good life. He was killed on Mark Antony's orders after opposing him.

books.title: On the Republic
books.note: The best constitution and the Dream of Scipio.

books.title: On Duties
books.note: Ethics of duty, for his son.

thinkers.quote: Philosophy is the guide of life.

thinkers.name: Lucretius
thinkers.bio: Lucretius was a Roman poet about whose life almost nothing is known. His single work sets out Epicurean physics and ethics in Latin verse. It aims to free readers from fear of the gods and death.
ideas: Natural origins of the world and society

books.title: De Rerum Natura
books.note: Epicurean physics in six books of verse.

thinkers.quote: Nothing can be created from nothing.
thinkers.start: De Rerum Natura (Stallings or Smith translation)

thinkers.name: Seneca
thinkers.bio: Seneca was a Stoic philosopher, dramatist and adviser to the emperor Nero. His letters and essays apply Stoicism to anger, grief, wealth and death. Accused of conspiracy, he was ordered by Nero to kill himself.

books.title: On the Shortness of Life
books.note: Life is long if you know how to use it.

thinkers.name: Epictetus
thinkers.bio: Epictetus was born a slave, later freed, and taught Stoicism at Nicopolis after philosophers were expelled from Rome. He wrote nothing; his pupil Arrian recorded his teachings. Central to them is distinguishing what is up to us from what is not.
thinkers.quote: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the opinions about things.

thinkers.name: Marcus Aurelius
thinkers.bio: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180. His private notebooks, written partly on military campaign, record Stoic self-exhortation. They were never meant for publication and became one of the most read philosophical books.

thinkers.name: Plotinus
thinkers.bio: Plotinus taught in Rome and founded Neoplatonism. Reality flows from the One through Intellect and Soul, and the soul can return to the One in contemplation. His pupil Porphyry arranged his treatises into the Enneads.
thinkers.quote: Never did eye see the sun unless it had first become sunlike, and never can the soul have vision of the First Beauty unless itself be beautiful.

thinkers.name: Sextus Empiricus
thinkers.bio: Sextus was a physician whose works are our main source for ancient Pyrrhonian skepticism. He set out modes of argument that produce suspension of judgment on any question. His rediscovery in the 16th century shaped Montaigne and early modern philosophy.

thinkers.name: Hypatia
thinkers.bio: Hypatia was a mathematician, astronomer and Neoplatonist teacher in Alexandria. She was admired for her learning and political influence. She was murdered by a Christian mob in 415; none of her writings survive with certainty.

thinkers.name: Laozi
thinkers.bio: Laozi is the traditional author of the Tao Te Ching and founder of Daoism. His historical existence is uncertain, and the text was probably compiled over time. It teaches harmony with the Dao through non-action, simplicity and yielding.

books.title: Tao Te Ching
books.note: 81 short chapters on the Way and its virtue.

thinkers.quote: The Tao that can be told is not the eternal Tao.
thinkers.start: Tao Te Ching (D. C. Lau translation)

thinkers.name: Confucius
thinkers.bio: Confucius was a teacher and minor official in the state of Lu. He taught that social harmony comes from cultivated moral character, ritual propriety and right relationships. His sayings were collected by disciples in the Analects and became the core of Chinese education for two millennia.

books.title: Analects
books.note: Sayings and dialogues collected by his disciples.

thinkers.quote: Learning without thought is labor lost; thought without learning is perilous.

thinkers.name: Mozi
thinkers.bio: Mozi founded Mohism, the main rival to Confucianism in the Warring States period. He argued for impartial care for all, against Confucian graded love, and condemned offensive war and wasteful ritual. Mohists also developed early logic and defensive military engineering.

books.title: Mozi
books.note: Collected writings of the Mohist school.

thinkers.name: Zhuangzi
thinkers.bio: Zhuangzi is the second great Daoist, known through the book bearing his name. With humour and parable he questions fixed perspectives, conventional values and the boundary between dreaming and waking. He celebrates spontaneous freedom and acceptance of transformation, including death.

thinkers.name: Mencius
thinkers.bio: Mencius was the most important Confucian after Confucius himself. He argued that human nature is good, containing sprouts of virtue that need cultivation. He held that rulers who oppress the people lose the Mandate of Heaven.

thinkers.name: Xunzi
thinkers.bio: Xunzi was a Confucian who held, against Mencius, that human nature is bad and must be shaped by ritual and learning. He saw Heaven as natural, not moral. His students included Han Feizi and Li Si.

books.title: Xunzi
books.note: Essays on ritual, learning and Heaven.

thinkers.quote: Heaven's ways are constant; it does not prevail because of a sage like Yao, nor perish because of a tyrant like Jie.

thinkers.name: Han Feizi
thinkers.bio: Han Feizi was a prince of the state of Han and the great synthesizer of Legalism. He argued that order comes from clear laws, rewards and punishments, and the ruler's techniques of control, not from virtue. His ideas influenced the Qin unification of China.

thinkers.name: Siddhartha Gautama
thinkers.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, renounced princely life and attained awakening. He taught the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path as a way to end suffering. His teaching rejects a permanent self and stresses dependent origination; it was transmitted orally before being written down.

books.title: Dhammapada
books.note: Verses of the Buddha's teaching (compiled later).

thinkers.quote: All conditioned things are impermanent; strive on with diligence.
thinkers.start: Walpola Rahula, What the Buddha Taught

thinkers.name: Nagarjuna
thinkers.bio: Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamaka (Middle Way) school of Mahayana Buddhism. He argued that all things are empty of intrinsic nature because they arise dependently. His dialectic shows that every fixed view leads to contradiction.

books.title: Mulamadhyamakakarika
books.note: Fundamental Verses on the Middle Way.

thinkers.start: Jay Garfield, The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way

thinkers.name: Vasubandhu
thinkers.bio: Vasubandhu wrote a major Abhidharma summary and then, according to tradition, converted to Mahayana under his half-brother Asanga. With Asanga he founded Yogacara, the "consciousness-only" school. His short verse treatises remain central in Indian and East Asian Buddhism.
thinkers.start: Jonathan Gold, Paving the Great Way

thinkers.name: Dharmakirti
thinkers.bio: Dharmakirti was the leading Buddhist logician and epistemologist. Building on Dignaga, he analyzed perception and inference as the only valid means of knowledge. His work dominated Indian and Tibetan debate for centuries.
thinkers.start: John Dunne, Foundations of Dharmakirti's Philosophy

thinkers.name: Adi Shankara
thinkers.bio: Shankara systematized Advaita (non-dual) Vedanta. He taught that Brahman alone is real, the world is appearance, and the self is identical with Brahman. He wrote commentaries on the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita and the Brahma Sutras.
thinkers.start: Eliot Deutsch, Advaita Vedanta: A Philosophical Reconstruction

thinkers.name: Ramanuja
thinkers.bio: Ramanuja was the main theologian of qualified non-dualism. Against Shankara, he held that the world and souls are real and form the body of God. He gave devotion (bhakti) to a personal god a philosophical basis.
thinkers.start: John Carman, The Theology of Ramanuja

thinkers.name: Zhu Xi
thinkers.bio: Zhu Xi synthesized Neo-Confucianism, combining principle (li) and vital energy (qi) in one metaphysics. He selected the Four Books as the core of Confucian learning. His commentaries became the basis of the imperial exams from 1313 to 1905.

books.title: Reflections on Things at Hand
books.note: Anthology of Neo-Confucian thought, with Lü Zuqian.

thinkers.start: Daniel Gardner, Learning to Be a Sage

thinkers.name: Wang Yangming
thinkers.bio: Wang Yangming was a scholar-official and general who founded the School of Mind. Against Zhu Xi, he held that principle is in the mind, not in external things. He taught the unity of knowledge and action and the innate knowing of the good.

thinkers.name: Dogen
thinkers.bio: Dogen studied Chan in China and founded the Soto school of Zen in Japan. He taught that seated meditation (zazen) is itself enlightenment, not a means to it. His essays explore time, being and Buddha-nature.

books.title: Shobogenzo
books.note: Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.

thinkers.start: Kazuaki Tanahashi (ed.), Moon in a Dewdrop

thinkers.name: Kitaro Nishida
thinkers.bio: Nishida founded the Kyoto School, bringing Zen and Western philosophy into dialogue. His first book grounded reality in "pure experience" prior to subject and object. He later developed a logic of place (basho) and absolute nothingness.
thinkers.quote: Pure experience is the moment of seeing a color or hearing a sound, prior to the distinction of subject and object.

thinkers.name: Keiji Nishitani
thinkers.bio: Nishitani studied with Nishida and Heidegger. He confronted European nihilism with the Buddhist idea of emptiness. He argued nihilism must be passed through, not avoided.

thinkers.name: D. T. Suzuki
thinkers.bio: Suzuki was the most influential interpreter of Zen to the West. His English books shaped the reception of Buddhism among writers, artists and psychologists. He taught at universities in Japan and the United States.

thinkers.name: Al-Kindi
thinkers.bio: Al-Kindi is called "the philosopher of the Arabs", the first major philosopher writing in Arabic. Working with translators in Baghdad, he adapted Greek philosophy to Islamic monotheism. He argued that philosophy and revelation agree, and he defended creation in time.
ideas: Philosophy as truth from any source

thinkers.name: Al-Farabi
thinkers.bio: Al-Farabi was known as the "Second Teacher" after Aristotle. He wrote commentaries on logic and a political philosophy modelled on Plato's Republic. His work shaped Avicenna, Maimonides and, in the twentieth century, Leo Strauss.

books.title: The Virtuous City
books.note: Principles of the opinions of the people of the virtuous city.

thinkers.quote: The virtuous city resembles a healthy body, all of whose limbs cooperate to make the life of the animal complete.
thinkers.start: Muhsin Mahdi, Alfarabi and the Foundation of Islamic Political Philosophy

thinkers.name: Avicenna
thinkers.bio: Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a physician and philosopher whose Canon of Medicine was used in Europe for centuries. He distinguished essence from existence and argued for a Necessary Existent. His "floating man" thought experiment argues for self-awareness independent of the body.

books.title: The Book of Healing
books.note: Encyclopedia of logic, physics and metaphysics.

thinkers.quote: Even suspended in midair with every sense cut off, a person would still affirm the existence of their own self.
thinkers.start: Peter Adamson, Philosophy in the Islamic World

thinkers.name: Al-Ghazali
thinkers.bio: Al-Ghazali was a jurist and theologian who taught at the Nizamiyya in Baghdad. After a spiritual crisis he left his post for years of Sufi practice. He attacked Avicennian philosophers on the world's eternity, God's knowledge and resurrection, while using their logic.

thinkers.name: Averroes
thinkers.bio: Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a judge and physician known in Latin Europe as "the Commentator" on Aristotle. He defended philosophy against al-Ghazali and argued that it is commanded by Islamic law for those able. Latin Averroism shaped debates at medieval Paris.

books.title: The Decisive Treatise
books.note: On harmony of law and philosophy.

thinkers.quote: Truth does not oppose truth, but agrees with it and bears witness to it.

thinkers.name: Ibn Arabi
thinkers.bio: Ibn Arabi was the most influential mystical thinker in Islam, known as "the greatest master". His vast writings develop the idea later called "unity of being". He influenced Sufism from Morocco to Indonesia.
ideas: Imagination as a mode of knowing
thinkers.start: William Chittick, Ibn Arabi: Heir to the Prophets

thinkers.name: Ibn Khaldun
thinkers.bio: Ibn Khaldun was a historian, judge and statesman in North Africa and Egypt. The introduction to his world history analyzes how dynasties rise and fall through social cohesion. He is often counted a forerunner of sociology and economics.
ideas: Social and economic causes in history

thinkers.name: Mulla Sadra
thinkers.bio: Mulla Sadra founded the "Transcendent Philosophy" synthesizing Avicenna, Suhrawardi's illuminationism, Sufism and theology. He argued for the primacy of existence over essence. He held that substance itself is in constant motion.
thinkers.start: Sajjad Rizvi, Mulla Sadra and Metaphysics

thinkers.name: Saadia Gaon
thinkers.bio: Saadia led the academy at Sura in Babylonia. He wrote the first systematic Jewish philosophy, arguing that reason and revelation agree. He also translated the Bible into Arabic.

thinkers.name: Maimonides
thinkers.bio: Maimonides was a rabbi, physician and philosopher who fled persecution in Spain and settled in Egypt. He codified Jewish law in the Mishneh Torah. In the Guide he reconciled Torah with Aristotle and wrote esoterically for the perplexed few.

books.title: The Guide for the Perplexed
books.note: Philosophy and the interpretation of scripture.

thinkers.quote: Accept the truth from whoever speaks it.

thinkers.name: Judah Halevi
thinkers.bio: Judah Halevi was a great Hebrew poet and a critic of philosophy. In the Kuzari, a Jewish sage persuades the Khazar king that history and revelation exceed philosophical reason. He died soon after travelling toward the Land of Israel.

thinkers.name: Augustine of Hippo
thinkers.bio: Augustine was a teacher of rhetoric who converted to Christianity in 386 and became bishop of Hippo. He merged Neoplatonism with Christian doctrine on God, the soul, evil and grace. His Confessions invented the inward spiritual autobiography, and The City of God answered pagan blame for the fall of Rome.
ideas: Time as distension of the mind

books.title: On the Trinity
books.note: The Trinity and the image of God in the mind.

books.title: The City of God
books.note: The earthly city versus the city of God.

thinkers.quote: You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.

thinkers.name: Boethius
thinkers.bio: Boethius was a Roman senator who served the Ostrogothic king Theodoric. He planned to translate all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin, and his logic translations shaped medieval education. Imprisoned on a charge of treason, he wrote the Consolation before his execution.

books.title: The Consolation of Philosophy
books.note: Lady Philosophy on fortune and providence.

thinkers.name: John Scotus Eriugena
thinkers.bio: Eriugena was an Irish scholar at the court of Charles the Bald. He translated Pseudo-Dionysius from Greek. His Periphyseon sets out a Neoplatonic division of nature in which all things come from and return to God.
thinkers.start: Dermot Moran, The Philosophy of John Scottus Eriugena

thinkers.name: Anselm of Canterbury
thinkers.bio: Anselm was a Benedictine monk and Archbishop of Canterbury. His motto was "faith seeking understanding". He gave the ontological argument: God is that than which nothing greater can be conceived, so God must exist in reality.

thinkers.name: Peter Abelard
thinkers.bio: Abelard was the most brilliant logician of the twelfth century and a celebrated teacher in Paris. His love affair with Heloise and its violent end became famous through their letters. He held that universals are words or concepts, and he stressed intention in ethics.

books.title: Sic et Non
books.note: Conflicting authorities set side by side.

thinkers.start: The Letters of Abelard and Heloise

thinkers.name: Hildegard of Bingen
thinkers.bio: Hildegard was a Benedictine abbess, visionary, composer and writer on medicine and nature. Her visionary works present a cosmic theology of creation and redemption. She was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.

thinkers.name: Thomas Aquinas
thinkers.bio: Aquinas was a Dominican friar who taught at Paris and Naples. He synthesized Aristotle with Christian theology, holding that reason and faith cannot conflict. His Summa Theologiae became the standard of Catholic theology, and he was canonized in 1323.

books.title: Summa contra Gentiles
books.note: Defence of the faith by reason.

thinkers.quote: Grace does not destroy nature, but perfects it.

thinkers.name: Bonaventure
thinkers.bio: Bonaventure was Minister General of the Franciscans and a contemporary of Aquinas at Paris. He kept a more Augustinian approach and criticized radical Aristotelianism. His Journey of the Mind to God traces an ascent through creatures to God.

books.title: The Journey of the Mind to God

thinkers.start: The Journey of the Mind to God

thinkers.name: John Duns Scotus
thinkers.bio: Duns Scotus was a Franciscan theologian known as the "Subtle Doctor". He argued that being is univocal, said in the same sense of God and creatures. He also proposed haecceity, "thisness", as what makes an individual itself.
thinkers.quote: Each individual possesses a 'thisness' (haecceitas) that makes it uniquely this being and no other.

thinkers.name: William of Ockham
thinkers.bio: Ockham was a Franciscan whose nominalism held that only individuals exist and universals are signs. His principle of parsimony became known as Ockham's razor. He clashed with Pope John XXII over apostolic poverty and fled to the protection of Emperor Louis IV.

thinkers.name: Meister Eckhart
thinkers.bio: Eckhart was a Dominican theologian and preacher. His German sermons speak of the birth of God in the soul and of letting go (Gelassenheit). Some of his propositions were condemned in 1329, after his death.
ideas: Birth of God in the soul

books.title: German Sermons
books.note: Vernacular sermons on detachment and union.

thinkers.name: Nicholas of Cusa
thinkers.bio: Nicholas of Cusa was a cardinal, mathematician and philosopher. He argued that God is beyond human reason, where opposites coincide, and that wisdom is learned ignorance. He also proposed that the universe has no fixed centre.

books.title: On Learned Ignorance
books.note: The limits of knowledge and the infinite.

thinkers.name: Marsilio Ficino
thinkers.bio: Ficino led the Florentine revival of Plato under Medici patronage. He translated all of Plato and Plotinus into Latin. His Platonic Theology argued for the immortality of the soul.

books.title: Platonic Theology
books.note: On the immortality of the soul.

thinkers.start: Paul Oskar Kristeller, The Philosophy of Marsilio Ficino

thinkers.name: Giovanni Pico della Mirandola
thinkers.bio: Pico planned a public debate of 900 theses drawn from many traditions, which the pope halted. His Oration presents humans as free to shape their own nature. He died at 31.

books.title: Oration on the Dignity of Man

thinkers.start: Oration on the Dignity of Man

thinkers.name: Desiderius Erasmus
thinkers.bio: Erasmus was the leading humanist scholar of northern Europe. He published a Greek New Testament and satirized clerical corruption. He sought church reform but broke with Luther over free will.

books.title: On Free Will
books.note: Defence of free will against Luther.

thinkers.name: Martin Luther
thinkers.bio: Luther was an Augustinian monk and theology professor whose 95 Theses (1517) sparked the Reformation. He taught justification by faith alone and the authority of scripture alone. His German Bible shaped the German language.

books.title: On the Bondage of the Will

thinkers.name: Niccolò Machiavelli
thinkers.bio: Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat removed from office when the Medici returned in 1512. In exile he wrote The Prince and the Discourses. He separated politics from traditional morality and analyzed power as it is.
ideas: Better to be feared than loved

books.title: The Prince
books.note: How principalities are won and kept.

thinkers.name: Thomas More
thinkers.bio: More was a humanist, lawyer and Lord Chancellor under Henry VIII. His Utopia describes an ideal island to criticize European society. He was executed for refusing to accept Henry as head of the Church.

books.title: Utopia
books.note: The ideal commonwealth of the island of Utopia.

thinkers.name: Michel de Montaigne
thinkers.bio: Montaigne retired from public life to write the Essays, inventing the essay form. He studied himself as an example of the human condition. Drawing on Sextus, he doubted human certainty and ridiculed cruelty and dogmatism.
thinkers.quote: Que sais-je? (What do I know?)

thinkers.name: Giordano Bruno
thinkers.bio: Bruno was a Dominican friar turned wandering philosopher. He defended an infinite universe with countless worlds, going beyond Copernicus. The Roman Inquisition burned him at the stake for heresy in 1600.

books.title: On the Infinite Universe and Worlds

thinkers.start: Frances Yates, Giordano Bruno and the Hermetic Tradition

thinkers.name: Francisco Suárez
thinkers.bio: Suárez was a Jesuit theologian whose Metaphysical Disputations was studied in Catholic and Protestant universities. He systematized scholastic metaphysics independent of commentary on Aristotle. He also wrote on law, natural law and the origin of political power.

thinkers.name: Francis Bacon
thinkers.bio: Bacon was a lawyer and Lord Chancellor of England. He called for a new method of science based on careful induction from experiment. He catalogued the "idols" that distort human understanding.

books.title: Novum Organum
books.note: New method; idols of the mind.

thinkers.start: Essays; then Novum Organum Book I

thinkers.name: Thomas Hobbes
thinkers.bio: Hobbes wrote during the English Civil War. He argued that without government life would be a war of all against all. To escape it, people covenant to give an absolute sovereign power. He was also a thoroughgoing materialist.

books.title: Leviathan
books.note: Sovereign power from the social contract.

thinkers.quote: The life of man, solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.

thinkers.name: Hugo Grotius
thinkers.bio: Grotius was a jurist who helped found international law. He argued that natural law would hold even if God did not exist. He escaped prison in a book chest.

books.title: On the Law of War and Peace

thinkers.start: On the Law of War and Peace, Prolegomena

thinkers.name: René Descartes
thinkers.bio: Descartes is called the father of modern philosophy. He sought certain foundations for knowledge by doubting everything doubtable and found the thinking self. He argued mind and body are distinct substances and helped found analytic geometry.
thinkers.quote: I think, therefore I am.

thinkers.name: Blaise Pascal
thinkers.bio: Pascal was a mathematician and physicist who built a calculating machine and contributed to probability theory. After a religious experience in 1654 he devoted himself to Christian apologetics. His unfinished notes were published as the Pensées.

books.title: Pensées
books.note: Fragments for a defence of Christianity.

thinkers.quote: The heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.

thinkers.name: Baruch Spinoza
thinkers.bio: Spinoza was expelled from Amsterdam's Jewish community in 1656 and earned a living grinding lenses. His Ethics, in geometrical form, identifies God with Nature as the one substance. He also defended freedom of thought and read the Bible historically.

books.title: Theological-Political Treatise
books.note: Freedom of thought and biblical criticism.

books.title: Ethics
books.note: God, mind and the affects in geometrical order.

thinkers.quote: God, or Nature.
thinkers.start: Ethics (Curley translation), Parts I and V

thinkers.name: John Locke
thinkers.bio: Locke was a physician and adviser to the Earl of Shaftesbury. He argued that all ideas come from experience. In politics, he held that government exists to protect natural rights and rests on consent, so revolution against tyranny is justified.
ideas: Natural rights to life, liberty and property
thinkers.quote: Where there is no law, there is no freedom.

thinkers.name: G. W. Leibniz
thinkers.bio: Leibniz was a diplomat, librarian and polymath who invented calculus independently of Newton. He held that reality consists of monads, simple mind-like substances in pre-established harmony. He argued this is the best of all possible worlds.

books.title: Theodicy
books.note: God and the problem of evil.

thinkers.quote: The monads have no windows through which anything can enter or depart.

thinkers.name: Nicolas Malebranche
thinkers.bio: Malebranche was an Oratorian priest who developed Descartes in a theological direction. He held that God is the only true cause and that we see all things in God. His work was widely read across Europe.

books.title: The Search after Truth
books.note: Errors and the method to avoid them.

thinkers.start: The Search after Truth, Book III

thinkers.name: Giambattista Vico
thinkers.bio: Vico was a professor of rhetoric in Naples. Against Descartes, he argued we can truly know only what we make, so history is more knowable than nature. He traced cycles of ages of gods, heroes and men.

books.title: The New Science
books.note: Principles of the common nature of nations.

thinkers.name: George Berkeley
thinkers.bio: Berkeley was an Anglican bishop. He argued that matter does not exist apart from perception; to be is to be perceived or to perceive. God's perception keeps things in being.

books.title: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous

thinkers.name: Montesquieu
thinkers.bio: Montesquieu was a magistrate and man of letters. In The Spirit of the Laws he related laws to climate, customs and regime type. His separation of powers shaped the American Constitution.

books.title: The Spirit of the Laws
books.note: Laws relative to climate and regime.

thinkers.start: The Spirit of the Laws, Book XI

thinkers.name: Voltaire
thinkers.bio: Voltaire was the most famous writer of the French Enlightenment. He campaigned against religious intolerance and injustice, as in the Calas affair. His satire Candide mocks Leibnizian optimism.

thinkers.name: David Hume
thinkers.bio: Hume was a philosopher, historian and essayist. He argued that causation is constant conjunction plus habit, raising the problem of induction. He held that reason serves the passions and that morality rests on sentiment.
thinkers.quote: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.

thinkers.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
thinkers.bio: Rousseau argued that civilization corrupted natural human goodness. In the Social Contract he proposed a sovereign general will expressing citizens' common good. His novels and autobiography helped launch Romanticism.
thinkers.quote: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.

thinkers.name: Denis Diderot
thinkers.bio: Diderot co-edited the Encyclopédie, a monument of the Enlightenment. He moved from deism to materialism. His dialogues and novels explored morality and nature.

thinkers.name: Adam Smith
thinkers.bio: Smith was a moral philosopher at Glasgow. His first book grounds morality in sympathy and an impartial spectator. His second analyzed division of labour, markets and free trade, founding modern economics.
thinkers.quote: It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.
thinkers.start: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Part I

thinkers.name: Immanuel Kant
thinkers.bio: Kant spent his life in Königsberg. Awoken from "dogmatic slumber" by Hume, he argued that space, time and categories structure experience, so we know appearances but not things in themselves. In ethics, he grounded morality in the categorical imperative and autonomy.

books.title: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
Perpetual Peace
books.note: Republics and a league of nations.

thinkers.quote: Two things fill the mind with ever new and increasing admiration and awe: the starry heavens above me and the moral law within me.
thinkers.start: Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals

thinkers.name: Edmund Burke
thinkers.bio: Burke was a Whig statesman in the British Parliament. He supported the American colonists but condemned the French Revolution. He defended tradition, prudence and inherited institutions over abstract rights.

books.title: A Philosophical Enquiry into the Sublime and Beautiful
Reflections on the Revolution in France

thinkers.quote: A state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.
thinkers.start: Reflections on the Revolution in France

thinkers.name: Jeremy Bentham
thinkers.bio: Bentham founded modern utilitarianism and was a legal and social reformer. He held that the right action produces the greatest happiness of the greatest number. He designed the Panopticon prison.

books.title: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation

thinkers.start: An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation, ch. 1–4

thinkers.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
thinkers.bio: Wollstonecraft was a writer and early advocate of women's rights. She argued that women appear inferior only because they lack education. She died after giving birth to Mary Shelley.
ideas: Reason and virtue for both sexes

books.title: A Vindication of the Rights of Men
A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

thinkers.start: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman

thinkers.name: Johann Gottfried Herder
thinkers.bio: Herder studied with Kant and influenced Goethe. He stressed that language and culture shape thought and that each people has its own character. He laid foundations for historicism and folk studies.

books.title: Treatise on the Origin of Language
Ideas for the Philosophy of History of Humanity

thinkers.name: Johann Georg Hamann
thinkers.bio: Hamann was Kant's friend and critic, called the "Magus of the North". He attacked Enlightenment reason in the name of faith, language and experience. He influenced Herder, Jacobi and Kierkegaard.
thinkers.start: Isaiah Berlin, The Magus of the North

thinkers.name: Christian Wolff
thinkers.bio: Wolff systematized Leibniz's philosophy and dominated German universities before Kant. He wrote textbooks in German and Latin covering all philosophy. Kant was trained in his system.

books.title: German Metaphysics
books.note: Rational thoughts on God, world and soul.

thinkers.start: Corey Dyck, Kant and Rational Psychology

thinkers.name: J. G. Fichte
thinkers.bio: Fichte radicalized Kant by deriving experience from the self-positing activity of the I. He was accused of atheism and lost his post at Jena. In the Addresses during Napoleonic occupation he called for national education.

books.title: Foundations of the Entire Science of Knowledge

thinkers.name: F. W. J. Schelling
thinkers.bio: Schelling was a prodigy who roomed with Hegel and Hölderlin at Tübingen. He developed a philosophy of nature and of identity, with art as the organ of philosophy. His late work on freedom and positive philosophy influenced Kierkegaard and existentialism.
ideas: Freedom and the ground of evil

books.title: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom

thinkers.start: Philosophical Investigations into the Essence of Human Freedom

thinkers.name: G. W. F. Hegel
thinkers.bio: Hegel was the most influential German Idealist and held the chair of philosophy in Berlin. He argued that reality is Spirit coming to know itself through history in a dialectical process. His philosophy of right and history shaped Marx, existentialism and much later thought.

books.title: Elements of the Philosophy of Right
books.note: Freedom in ethical life and the state.

books.title: Lectures on the Philosophy of History
books.note: History as the progress of freedom.

thinkers.quote: The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of dusk.
thinkers.start: Introduction to the Lectures on the Philosophy of History

thinkers.name: Friedrich Hölderlin
thinkers.bio: Hölderlin was a poet and friend of Hegel and Schelling. His fragment "Judgment and Being" influenced early idealism. His poetry was central for Heidegger.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Schleiermacher
thinkers.bio: Schleiermacher was a theologian and translator of Plato. He defined religion as the feeling of absolute dependence. He founded general hermeneutics.

books.title: On Religion: Speeches to Its Cultured Despisers

thinkers.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
thinkers.bio: Schopenhauer held that the thing-in-itself behind representation is a blind, striving Will. Life is therefore suffering, relieved by art, compassion and ascetic denial of the will. He drew on Indian thought and influenced Nietzsche, Wagner and Wittgenstein.

books.title: The World as Will and Representation

thinkers.quote: The world is my representation.

thinkers.name: Ludwig Feuerbach
thinkers.bio: Feuerbach studied with Hegel and became a leading Young Hegelian. He argued that God is a projection of idealized human nature. His humanist materialism influenced Marx and Engels.

thinkers.name: Max Stirner
thinkers.bio: Max Stirner was the pen name of Johann Kaspar Schmidt, a schoolteacher in Berlin's Young Hegelian circle. His one major book attacks God, humanity, the state and morality as "spooks" that subordinate the individual. Marx and Engels wrote a long polemic against him in The German Ideology. He died in poverty.

books.title: The Ego and Its Own
books.note: Der Einzige und sein Eigentum; against all fixed ideas.

thinkers.quote: I have set my cause on nothing.
thinkers.start: The Ego and Its Own (Leopold edition)

thinkers.name: Søren Kierkegaard
thinkers.bio: Kierkegaard wrote under many pseudonyms to show different stances toward life. He attacked Hegel's system and the comfortable Christendom of Denmark. He stressed the individual's passionate choice and the leap of faith.

books.title: Fear and Trembling
books.note: Abraham and the leap of faith.

thinkers.quote: Life can only be understood backwards; but it must be lived forwards.

thinkers.name: Auguste Comte
thinkers.bio: Comte founded positivism and coined the word "sociology". He held that thought passes through theological, metaphysical and positive stages. Late in life he founded a "Religion of Humanity".

thinkers.name: John Stuart Mill
thinkers.bio: Mill was educated intensively by his father James Mill and Bentham. He refined utilitarianism with higher and lower pleasures. He defended individual liberty, representative government and women's equality.

books.title: The Subjection of Women
books.note: For legal equality of the sexes.

thinkers.quote: It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.

thinkers.name: Karl Marx
thinkers.bio: Marx was a philosopher, economist and revolutionary who spent most of his life in exile in London. With Engels, he developed historical materialism: history is driven by class struggle over the means of production. His Capital analyzed how capitalism extracts surplus value from labour.

books.title: The German Ideology
books.note: With Engels; includes attack on Stirner.

thinkers.quote: The philosophers have only interpreted the world, in various ways; the point is to change it.
thinkers.start: The Communist Manifesto, then Capital ch. 1

thinkers.name: Friedrich Engels
thinkers.bio: Engels was a factory manager's son and Marx's lifelong collaborator and funder. He described working conditions in Manchester. He edited Capital's later volumes.

books.title: The Condition of the Working Class in England

thinkers.name: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon
thinkers.bio: Proudhon was the first to call himself an anarchist. He argued property in the sense of rent and interest is theft. He proposed mutualism and federalism.
thinkers.quote: Property is theft.

thinkers.name: Mikhail Bakunin
thinkers.bio: Bakunin was a revolutionary anarchist who clashed with Marx in the First International. He opposed all state power, including a workers' state. He was imprisoned and escaped from Siberia.

thinkers.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
thinkers.bio: Emerson left the ministry to become a lecturer and essayist. He led American Transcendentalism, teaching self-reliance and the divinity of nature. Nietzsche admired him.

thinkers.name: Henry David Thoreau
thinkers.bio: Thoreau lived two years in a cabin at Walden Pond. He refused to pay a poll tax supporting slavery and war. His essay on civil disobedience influenced Gandhi and King.

thinkers.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
thinkers.bio: Dostoevsky was a novelist who survived a mock execution and Siberian labour camp. His novels probe freedom, guilt, faith and nihilism. He is a major precursor of existentialism.

books.title: The Brothers Karamazov
books.note: Faith, doubt and the Grand Inquisitor.

thinkers.name: Leo Tolstoy
thinkers.bio: Tolstoy was the author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina. After a spiritual crisis he preached nonviolence and a rational Christianity without church dogma. He influenced Gandhi.

books.title: The Kingdom of God Is Within You

thinkers.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
thinkers.bio: Nietzsche became a professor of classical philology at Basel at 24 and left in 1879 due to ill health. In aphoristic books he diagnosed the "death of God" and the danger of nihilism. He called for a revaluation of all values. He collapsed in 1889 and spent his last decade incapacitated.

books.title: Beyond Good and Evil
books.note: Prelude to a philosophy of the future.

books.title: Twilight of the Idols
books.note: How to philosophize with a hammer.

thinkers.quote: God is dead.

thinkers.name: Wilhelm Dilthey
thinkers.bio: Dilthey distinguished the human sciences, aimed at understanding, from the natural sciences, aimed at explanation. He developed hermeneutics and a philosophy of lived experience. Heidegger and Gadamer built on him.

thinkers.name: Franz Brentano
thinkers.bio: Brentano was a priest who left the Church over papal infallibility. He revived intentionality, the directedness of mind to objects. His students included Husserl, and Freud attended his lectures.

books.title: Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint
books.note: Intentionality as the mark of the mental.

thinkers.start: Psychology from an Empirical Standpoint, Book II ch. 1

thinkers.name: C. S. Peirce
thinkers.bio: Peirce was a logician, scientist and founder of pragmatism. He developed semiotics and abductive reasoning. He never held a permanent academic post and died poor.

books.title: How to Make Our Ideas Clear

thinkers.name: William James
thinkers.bio: James was a physician turned psychologist and philosopher at Harvard. He popularized pragmatism and wrote a founding text of psychology. He defended the right to believe and studied religious experience.
thinkers.quote: Truth happens to an idea. It becomes true, is made true by events.

thinkers.name: Henry Sidgwick
thinkers.bio: Sidgwick was a Cambridge philosopher whose Methods of Ethics compared egoism, intuitionism and utilitarianism. Parfit and Singer regarded it as among the best books in ethics. He also promoted women's education.
ideas: Point of view of the universe

thinkers.name: Gottlob Frege
thinkers.bio: Frege was a mathematician at Jena who invented modern predicate logic. He tried to derive arithmetic from logic, a project wrecked by Russell's paradox. His distinction between sense and reference founded philosophy of language.

thinkers.name: Bertrand Russell
thinkers.bio: Russell co-founded analytic philosophy and wrote Principia Mathematica with Whitehead. His theory of descriptions became a model of philosophical analysis. He was jailed as a pacifist in World War I, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1950 and campaigned against nuclear weapons.
thinkers.quote: The good life is one inspired by love and guided by knowledge.

thinkers.name: G. E. Moore
thinkers.bio: Moore led the Cambridge revolt against British idealism with Russell. He defended common-sense beliefs and argued that "good" is a simple, indefinable property. His ethics influenced the Bloomsbury Group.

thinkers.name: Alfred North Whitehead
thinkers.bio: Whitehead was a mathematician who co-wrote Principia Mathematica with Russell. At Harvard he developed process philosophy, in which reality consists of events of becoming. He criticized the "fallacy of misplaced concreteness".
thinkers.quote: The safest general characterization of the European philosophical tradition is that it consists of a series of footnotes to Plato.

thinkers.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
thinkers.bio: Wittgenstein came from one of Vienna's wealthiest families and studied with Russell at Cambridge. He wrote the Tractatus while a soldier in World War I, then gave up philosophy for years. Returning to Cambridge, he rejected his early views and argued that meaning is use within language-games.
ideas: What cannot be said must be shown

books.title: Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus
books.note: Picture theory; the limits of language.

thinkers.quote: Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.
thinkers.start: Ray Monk, The Duty of Genius; then Philosophical Investigations

thinkers.name: Frank Ramsey
thinkers.bio: Ramsey made lasting contributions to logic, probability, economics and philosophy before dying at 26. He helped translate the Tractatus and persuaded Wittgenstein to return to philosophy. His subjective theory of probability anticipated decision theory.
thinkers.start: Cheryl Misak, Frank Ramsey: A Sheer Excess of Powers

thinkers.name: Rudolf Carnap
thinkers.bio: Carnap was a leading member of the Vienna Circle. He tried to reconstruct knowledge logically from experience and argued metaphysics is meaningless. After emigrating to the US, he worked on semantics and inductive logic.

books.title: The Logical Structure of the World

thinkers.quote: In logic, there are no morals. Everyone is at liberty to build up his own logic.

thinkers.name: A. J. Ayer
thinkers.bio: Ayer brought Vienna Circle ideas to Britain at 26. He held that statements are meaningful only if analytic or empirically verifiable. Ethical statements, on his view, express emotions.

thinkers.name: Karl Popper
thinkers.bio: Popper argued that science advances by bold conjectures and attempted refutations, not induction. A theory is scientific only if falsifiable. Written in New Zealand exile, his Open Society attacked Plato, Hegel and Marx as enemies of freedom.

books.title: The Open Society and Its Enemies

thinkers.quote: The criterion of the scientific status of a theory is its falsifiability, or refutability, or testability.

thinkers.name: Gilbert Ryle
thinkers.bio: Ryle was an Oxford philosopher and editor of Mind. He attacked Cartesian dualism as "the dogma of the ghost in the machine". He distinguished knowing how from knowing that.

thinkers.name: J. L. Austin
thinkers.bio: Austin led Oxford ordinary language philosophy. He showed that utterances do things, like promising or marrying. His speech act theory was developed by Searle.

books.title: How to Do Things with Words

thinkers.start: How to Do Things with Words

thinkers.name: G. E. M. Anscombe
thinkers.bio: Anscombe was Wittgenstein's student, literary executor and translator. Her Intention founded modern action theory. Her essay "Modern Moral Philosophy" helped revive virtue ethics.

thinkers.name: W. V. O. Quine
thinkers.bio: Quine taught at Harvard for decades. He attacked the analytic-synthetic distinction and held that beliefs face experience as a whole web. He argued epistemology should become part of psychology.

books.title: On What There Is
books.note: To be is to be the value of a variable.

thinkers.quote: To be is to be the value of a variable.
thinkers.start: From a Logical Point of View

thinkers.name: Wilfrid Sellars
thinkers.bio: Sellars taught at Pittsburgh. He attacked the "Myth of the Given", the idea that knowledge rests on self-justifying experience. He contrasted the manifest and scientific images of man.

books.title: Empiricism and the Philosophy of Mind
Philosophy and the Scientific Image of Man

thinkers.start: Philosophy and the Scientific Image of Man

thinkers.name: Donald Davidson
thinkers.bio: Davidson argued that reasons are causes of actions. He developed a truth-conditional theory of meaning and radical interpretation. He held anomalous monism about mind.

thinkers.name: Thomas Kuhn
thinkers.bio: Kuhn trained as a physicist before turning to history of science. He argued science alternates between normal science under a paradigm and revolutions. His book popularized "paradigm shift".

thinkers.name: Paul Feyerabend
thinkers.bio: Feyerabend was a student of Popper who turned against all fixed scientific method. He argued that the history of science shows "anything goes". He defended pluralism.

thinkers.name: John Rawls
thinkers.bio: Rawls taught at Harvard and revived normative political philosophy. He asked what principles people would choose behind a veil of ignorance. He concluded with equal basic liberties and the difference principle.
ideas: Original position and veil of ignorance

thinkers.name: Robert Nozick
thinkers.bio: Nozick was a Harvard colleague of Rawls. His first book defended a minimal state limited to protecting rights. It introduced the experience machine and the Wilt Chamberlain argument.
thinkers.start: Anarchy, State, and Utopia, Part II

thinkers.name: Saul Kripke
thinkers.bio: Kripke developed possible-world semantics for modal logic as a teenager. His lectures "Naming and Necessity" argued names are rigid designators and that there are necessary truths known a posteriori. He also gave an influential reading of Wittgenstein on rules.

books.title: Wittgenstein on Rules and Private Language

thinkers.quote: A proper name is a rigid designator, designating the same object in every possible world.

thinkers.name: David Lewis
thinkers.bio: Lewis taught at Princeton. He defended modal realism, the view that possible worlds are as real as ours. He wrote influential work on counterfactuals, convention and mind.

thinkers.name: Hilary Putnam
thinkers.bio: Putnam taught at Harvard and often changed his views publicly. He argued "meanings ain't in the head" with Twin Earth. He proposed functionalism and later criticized it.

thinkers.name: Richard Rorty
thinkers.bio: Rorty was trained as an analytic philosopher but turned against its foundational ambitions. He argued that knowledge is not a mirror of nature. He championed pragmatism, liberal irony and conversation.

books.title: Philosophy and the Mirror of Nature

thinkers.name: Alasdair MacIntyre
thinkers.bio: MacIntyre moved from Marxism to Aristotelian Thomism. He argued modern moral discourse is fragments of a lost tradition. He called for communities of virtue.

thinkers.name: Bernard Williams
thinkers.bio: Williams was a critic of utilitarianism and Kantian moral theory. He coined "moral luck" and stressed integrity and ground projects. He thought ethics needs history and Greek thought.

books.title: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy

thinkers.quote: Ethical life is far richer and more complex than any single system of morality.
thinkers.start: Ethics and the Limits of Philosophy

thinkers.name: Derek Parfit
thinkers.bio: Parfit spent his career at All Souls College, Oxford. He argued personal identity is not what matters in survival. He also pioneered population ethics.

thinkers.name: Peter Singer
thinkers.bio: Singer is a utilitarian who has taught at Princeton. His Animal Liberation launched the modern animal rights movement. He argues the affluent have strong duties to help the global poor.

thinkers.name: Thomas Nagel
thinkers.bio: Nagel taught at New York University. He argued that consciousness has a subjective character physics cannot capture. He also wrote on objectivity and moral luck.

books.title: What Is It Like to Be a Bat?

thinkers.name: John Searle
thinkers.bio: Searle developed speech act theory after Austin. His Chinese Room argued that running a program does not produce understanding. He wrote on social reality.

thinkers.name: Daniel Dennett
thinkers.bio: Dennett studied with Ryle at Oxford and taught at Tufts. He defended a naturalistic, deflationary account of consciousness. He was a prominent advocate of Darwinism and atheism.
thinkers.start: Intuition Pumps and Other Tools for Thinking

thinkers.name: David Chalmers
thinkers.bio: Chalmers formulated the "hard problem" of consciousness. He argues consciousness cannot be reduced to physical processes. He co-proposed the extended mind thesis with Andy Clark.

thinkers.name: Martha Nussbaum
thinkers.bio: Nussbaum works on ancient philosophy, ethics, law and the emotions. With Amartya Sen she developed the capabilities approach. She teaches at the University of Chicago.

thinkers.name: Charles Taylor
thinkers.bio: Taylor is a Canadian philosopher of the self, politics and religion. He criticized atomistic liberalism. His Secular Age traces how belief became optional.

thinkers.name: Roger Scruton
thinkers.bio: Scruton was a philosopher of aesthetics and leading conservative thinker. He wrote on beauty, music, architecture and home. He supported dissident intellectuals behind the Iron Curtain.

thinkers.name: Mark Fisher
thinkers.bio: Fisher was a writer and teacher who blogged as k-punk. His Capitalist Realism argued it is easier to imagine the end of the world than of capitalism. He also wrote on hauntology in music.

thinkers.name: John Dewey
thinkers.bio: Dewey was the leading pragmatist of the twentieth century and a public intellectual. He saw thinking as inquiry for solving problems in experience. He championed progressive education and democracy as a way of life.
ideas: Democracy as a way of life

thinkers.name: George Santayana
thinkers.bio: Santayana was raised in Spain and Boston and taught at Harvard until 1912. He combined naturalism with a love of beauty and religion as poetry. He spent his later life in Europe.
thinkers.quote: Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.

thinkers.name: Henri Bergson
thinkers.bio: Bergson was the most famous French philosopher of his time and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1927. He contrasted lived duration with spatialized clock time. He proposed a creative vital impulse (élan vital) in evolution.
thinkers.quote: To exist is to change, to change is to mature, to mature is to go on creating oneself endlessly.

thinkers.name: Edmund Husserl
thinkers.bio: Husserl began as a mathematician and became the founder of phenomenology. He sought to describe the structures of consciousness by bracketing assumptions about the world. Born Jewish (he became a Lutheran), he was barred from the university under the Nazis.
thinkers.quote: Back to the things themselves!

thinkers.name: Max Scheler
thinkers.bio: Scheler applied phenomenology to ethics, values and emotion. He argued that values are given in feeling and ranked objectively. He also founded philosophical anthropology.

books.title: Formalism in Ethics and Non-Formal Ethics of Values

thinkers.name: Martin Heidegger
thinkers.bio: Heidegger studied with Husserl and returned to the question of the meaning of Being. Being and Time analyzed human existence as Dasein: being-in-the-world, care, and being-toward-death. He joined the Nazi party in 1933 as rector of Freiburg, which remains deeply controversial. His later work turned to language, poetry and technology.

books.title: Introduction to Metaphysics
books.note: Why is there something rather than nothing?

thinkers.quote: Language is the house of Being.
thinkers.start: Basic Writings (Krell), then Being and Time

thinkers.name: Karl Jaspers
thinkers.bio: Jaspers was a psychiatrist turned philosopher. He explored existence through "limit situations" such as death, guilt and struggle. He mentored Hannah Arendt and wrote on German guilt after the war.

books.title: The Origin and Goal of History

thinkers.name: Gabriel Marcel
thinkers.bio: Marcel was a playwright and Catholic existentialist. He distinguished problems from mysteries. He stressed hope, fidelity and presence.

thinkers.name: Nikolai Berdyaev
thinkers.bio: Berdyaev was a Russian religious philosopher expelled by the Bolsheviks in 1922. In Paris he wrote on freedom, creativity and personality. Freedom, he held, precedes being.

books.title: The Meaning of the Creative Act

thinkers.name: José Ortega y Gasset
thinkers.bio: Ortega was Spain's leading philosopher and a public essayist. He held that "I am I and my circumstance". His Revolt of the Masses diagnosed the rise of mass man.
ideas: I am I and my circumstance

thinkers.name: Miguel de Unamuno
thinkers.bio: Unamuno was a novelist, poet and rector of Salamanca. He wrote of the hunger for immortality against reason's doubts. He publicly defied Francoist officers in 1936.

books.title: The Tragic Sense of Life
books.note: Reason versus the longing for immortality.

thinkers.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
thinkers.bio: Sartre was the leading figure of French existentialism, as novelist, dramatist and philosopher. He held that existence precedes essence: humans are condemned to be free and define themselves by acts. He declined the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1964 and moved toward Marxism.
thinkers.quote: Hell is other people.

thinkers.name: Simone de Beauvoir
thinkers.bio: Beauvoir was a philosopher and novelist and Sartre's lifelong partner. The Second Sex argued that woman has been made the Other. It became a founding text of second-wave feminism.
ideas: One is not born a woman
thinkers.quote: One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.

thinkers.name: Albert Camus
thinkers.bio: Camus was a novelist, essayist and Resistance journalist. He described the absurd: the clash between our need for meaning and a silent universe. He rejected suicide and nihilism in favour of revolt and won the Nobel Prize in 1957.
thinkers.quote: One must imagine Sisyphus happy.

thinkers.name: Maurice Merleau-Ponty
thinkers.bio: Merleau-Ponty held the chair at the Collège de France. He put the lived body at the centre of perception. He co-edited Les Temps Modernes with Sartre before breaking with him.

thinkers.name: Emmanuel Levinas
thinkers.bio: Levinas studied with Husserl and Heidegger. Much of his family was killed in the Holocaust, and he was a prisoner of war. He argued that ethics, the face-to-face with the Other, is first philosophy.

thinkers.name: Hans-Georg Gadamer
thinkers.bio: Gadamer studied with Heidegger. His Truth and Method made hermeneutics a general philosophy of understanding. He held that tradition and prejudice make understanding possible.

thinkers.name: Paul Ricœur
thinkers.bio: Ricoeur combined phenomenology and hermeneutics. He wrote on the will, symbol, metaphor, narrative and memory. He coined the "hermeneutics of suspicion" for Marx, Nietzsche and Freud.

thinkers.name: Simone Weil
thinkers.bio: Weil was a philosopher, labour activist and mystic. She worked in factories and joined the Spanish Civil War. She died in England while with the Free French; most of her work was published posthumously.

thinkers.name: Georges Bataille
thinkers.bio: Bataille was a librarian and writer on eroticism, sacrifice and excess. He argued societies are shaped by how they spend surplus energy. He influenced Foucault, Derrida and Baudrillard.

thinkers.name: Emil Cioran
thinkers.bio: Cioran wrote early books in Romanian and settled in Paris, writing in French from 1949. His aphorisms express pessimism, insomnia and lucid despair. He renounced his youthful far-right sympathies.

thinkers.name: René Girard
thinkers.bio: Girard taught at Stanford and Johns Hopkins. He argued desire is mimetic: we desire what others desire. Rivalry is resolved by the scapegoat mechanism behind religion and culture.

books.title: Things Hidden Since the Foundation of the World

thinkers.start: I See Satan Fall Like Lightning

thinkers.name: Carl Schmitt
thinkers.bio: Schmitt was a jurist and critic of liberal parliamentarism. He defined sovereignty as deciding on the exception and the political as the friend-enemy distinction. He joined the Nazi party in 1933, which permanently stained his reputation. His work remains influential on the left and right.
thinkers.quote: Sovereign is he who decides on the exception.

thinkers.name: Leo Strauss
thinkers.bio: Strauss left Germany in 1932 and taught for decades at the University of Chicago. He argued that earlier philosophers often wrote esoterically to avoid persecution. He sought to revive classical political philosophy against modern historicism and relativism.

books.title: Persecution and the Art of Writing

thinkers.quote: Political philosophy is the attempt to replace opinion about the nature of political things by knowledge of the nature of political things.

thinkers.name: Hannah Arendt
thinkers.bio: Arendt studied with Heidegger and Jaspers and fled Nazi Germany in 1933. Her Origins of Totalitarianism analyzed Nazism and Stalinism. Reporting on Eichmann's trial, she coined "the banality of evil".
thinkers.quote: The sad truth is that most evil is done by people who never make up their minds to be good or evil.

thinkers.name: Eric Voegelin
thinkers.bio: Voegelin fled Austria in 1938. He studied the history of order and its symbols. He described modern mass movements as gnostic attempts to immanentize the eschaton.

thinkers.name: Alexandre Kojève
thinkers.bio: Kojève lectured on Hegel in Paris in the 1930s to Lacan, Bataille, Merleau-Ponty and others. He read history through the master-slave dialectic and its end. After the war he became a senior French trade official.

books.title: Introduction to the Reading of Hegel
books.note: Master-slave and the end of history.

thinkers.quote: Human desire is the desire of the desire of another.
thinkers.start: Introduction to the Reading of Hegel

thinkers.name: Ernst Jünger
thinkers.bio: Jünger was a decorated WWI officer whose war memoir made him famous. He described a coming age of total mobilization and the worker. He kept his distance from the Nazis and later wrote on inner freedom.

thinkers.name: René Guénon
thinkers.bio: Guénon founded the Traditionalist school. He held that a primordial tradition underlies all religions and that modernity is decline. He converted to Islam and lived in Cairo.

books.title: The Crisis of the Modern World
The Reign of Quantity and the Signs of the Times

thinkers.start: The Crisis of the Modern World

thinkers.name: Julius Evola
thinkers.bio: Evola was an esotericist and Traditionalist writer. His critique of modernity was tied to racial and far-right politics. He remains influential and controversial on the far right.
thinkers.start: Revolt Against the Modern World (read critically)

thinkers.name: Aleksandr Dugin
thinkers.bio: Dugin is a controversial Russian theorist of Eurasianism. He draws on Heidegger, Schmitt and Traditionalism to oppose liberalism. His political influence is debated.

thinkers.name: Isaiah Berlin
thinkers.bio: Berlin was an Oxford historian of ideas. He distinguished negative from positive liberty. He defended value pluralism.

thinkers.name: Friedrich Hayek
thinkers.bio: Hayek was an economist of the Austrian school and Nobel laureate in 1974. He argued central planning cannot use dispersed knowledge. He defended spontaneous order and the rule of law.

books.title: The Use of Knowledge in Society

thinkers.start: The Use of Knowledge in Society

thinkers.name: Michael Oakeshott
thinkers.bio: Oakeshott taught at the LSE. He criticized rationalism in politics and defended practical knowledge and civil association.

thinkers.name: Walter Benjamin
thinkers.bio: Benjamin was a critic and essayist linked to the Frankfurt School. He wrote on art, history, translation and the arcades of Paris. Fleeing the Nazis, he died at the Spanish border in 1940.

books.title: The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction
Theses on the Philosophy of History

thinkers.name: Max Horkheimer
thinkers.bio: Horkheimer directed the Institute for Social Research. He defined critical theory against traditional theory. With Adorno he wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment.

thinkers.name: Theodor Adorno
thinkers.bio: Adorno was a philosopher, sociologist and musicologist. In exile he and Horkheimer argued that enlightenment reason turns into domination. He criticized the culture industry.
thinkers.quote: Wrong life cannot be lived rightly.

thinkers.name: Herbert Marcuse
thinkers.bio: Marcuse studied with Heidegger before joining the Frankfurt School. In America he became a hero of the New Left. He argued advanced capitalism produces one-dimensional thought.

thinkers.name: Jürgen Habermas
thinkers.bio: Habermas is the leading heir of the Frankfurt School. He grounds critique in communicative rationality aimed at mutual understanding. He has defended modernity and deliberative democracy.

books.title: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere

thinkers.quote: No force except that of the better argument is exercised.
thinkers.start: The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere

thinkers.name: Antonio Gramsci
thinkers.bio: Gramsci co-founded the Italian Communist Party and was imprisoned by Mussolini. In prison notebooks he developed the concept of cultural hegemony. He died shortly after release.

thinkers.name: György Lukács
thinkers.bio: Lukács founded Western Marxism with History and Class Consciousness. He developed reification as a key concept. He later wrote on realism in literature.

thinkers.name: Sigmund Freud
thinkers.bio: Freud founded psychoanalysis in Vienna. He held that unconscious desires shape mind and culture. He fled the Nazis in 1938 and died in London.
thinkers.quote: Where id was, there ego shall be.

thinkers.name: Jacques Lacan
thinkers.bio: Lacan reread Freud with structural linguistics. He held that the unconscious is structured like a language. His seminars influenced Althusser, Žižek and literary theory.
thinkers.quote: The unconscious is structured like a language.
thinkers.start: Bruce Fink, A Clinical Introduction to Lacanian Psychoanalysis

thinkers.name: Claude Lévi-Strauss
thinkers.bio: Lévi-Strauss founded structural anthropology. He analyzed kinship and myth as systems of binary oppositions. He was a critic of Sartre's historicism.

thinkers.name: Louis Althusser
thinkers.bio: Althusser taught at the École normale supérieure. He read Marx structurally against humanism. In 1980 he killed his wife and was declared unfit to stand trial.

thinkers.name: Michel Foucault
thinkers.bio: Foucault held a chair at the Collège de France. He wrote histories of madness, medicine, prisons and sexuality. He showed how power and knowledge produce subjects. He died of AIDS-related illness.
thinkers.quote: Where there is power, there is resistance.

thinkers.name: Gilles Deleuze
thinkers.bio: Deleuze wrote studies of Hume, Nietzsche, Bergson and Spinoza. He built a philosophy of difference and becoming. With Félix Guattari he wrote Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus.
thinkers.quote: Philosophy is the art of forming, inventing, and fabricating concepts.

thinkers.name: Félix Guattari
thinkers.bio: Guattari was a psychoanalyst at La Borde clinic and political activist. He co-wrote Anti-Oedipus and A Thousand Plateaus with Deleuze. He developed schizoanalysis.

thinkers.name: Jacques Derrida
thinkers.bio: Derrida founded deconstruction. He showed how texts depend on oppositions they cannot stabilize. He wrote on writing, justice, hospitality and Marx.
thinkers.quote: There is nothing outside the text.

thinkers.name: Jean-François Lyotard
thinkers.bio: Lyotard defined the postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives. He also wrote on the sublime and the differend.

thinkers.name: Jean Baudrillard
thinkers.bio: Baudrillard was a sociologist of consumer society. He argued signs have replaced reality with simulation. His provocations included "The Gulf War Did Not Take Place".

thinkers.name: Alain Badiou
thinkers.bio: Badiou identifies ontology with set theory. He defines truths as fidelity to events in politics, science, art and love. He remains a committed Maoist-influenced militant.
thinkers.start: Ethics: An Essay on the Understanding of Evil

thinkers.name: Giorgio Agamben
thinkers.bio: Agamben combines Heidegger, Benjamin, Schmitt and Foucault. He studies sovereignty and bare life. He argued the state of exception has become the norm.

thinkers.name: Peter Sloterdijk
thinkers.bio: Sloterdijk is a German philosopher and cultural theorist. He became famous with Critique of Cynical Reason. His Spheres trilogy studies human spaces.

thinkers.name: Nick Land
thinkers.bio: Land taught at Warwick and co-founded the CCRU. His writings fuse Deleuze, Bataille and cyberculture into accelerationism. He later moved to Shanghai and the neoreactionary right.

thinkers.name: Slavoj Žižek
thinkers.bio: Žižek combines Hegel, Lacan and Marx in critiques of ideology. He writes prolifically on politics and popular culture.

thinkers.name: Judith Butler
thinkers.bio: Butler teaches at Berkeley. Their Gender Trouble argued gender is performative. They write on vulnerability and ethics.

thinkers.name: Frantz Fanon
thinkers.bio: Fanon was a psychiatrist who served in Algeria and joined the independence struggle. He analyzed the psychology of colonialism and racism. He died of leukemia at 36.

thinkers.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
thinkers.bio: Du Bois was the first African American to earn a Harvard PhD. He co-founded the NAACP. He described double consciousness and the colour line.
thinkers.quote: The problem of the twentieth century is the problem of the color-line.

thinkers.name: Frederick Douglass
thinkers.bio: Douglass escaped slavery in 1838 and became a leading abolitionist orator. His autobiographies are classics of American letters. He argued the Constitution could be read as anti-slavery.

books.title: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

thinkers.start: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

thinkers.name: Kwasi Wiredu
thinkers.bio: Wiredu was a leading African philosopher trained at Oxford under Ryle. He called for "conceptual decolonization". He studied Akan thought.

thinkers.name: Léopold Sédar Senghor
thinkers.bio: Senghor was a poet and first president of Senegal. With Césaire he developed Négritude. He was elected to the Académie française.

thinkers.name: Aimé Césaire
thinkers.bio: Césaire was a poet and politician. He co-founded Négritude. His Discourse on Colonialism condemned European colonialism. He taught Fanon.

thinkers.name: Enrique Dussel
thinkers.bio: Dussel was a founder of the philosophy of liberation. He drew on Levinas and Marx. He wrote from the standpoint of the excluded.

thinkers.name: Paulo Freire
thinkers.bio: Freire was an educator who taught literacy to Brazilian peasants. He criticized the "banking" model of education. He was exiled after the 1964 coup.

thinkers.name: José Vasconcelos
thinkers.bio: Vasconcelos was Mexico's education minister and a philosopher. He promoted public education and muralism. He proposed a "cosmic race".

thinkers.name: Octavio Paz
thinkers.bio: Paz was a poet, essayist and diplomat who won the 1990 Nobel Prize in Literature. His Labyrinth of Solitude probed Mexican identity.

thinkers.name: Nicolás Gómez Dávila
thinkers.bio: Gómez Dávila was a reclusive Colombian writer of aphorisms. He was a reactionary critic of modernity.

thinkers.name: Mahatma Gandhi
thinkers.bio: Gandhi led India's independence movement through nonviolent resistance. He drew on Hindu, Jain and Christian sources, and on Tolstoy and Thoreau. He was assassinated in 1948.

thinkers.name: Sri Aurobindo
thinkers.bio: Aurobindo was a nationalist turned yogi and philosopher. He described an evolution of consciousness. He founded an ashram in Pondicherry.

thinkers.name: Muhammad Iqbal
thinkers.bio: Iqbal was a poet-philosopher who studied in Cambridge and Munich. He argued for a dynamic reconstruction of Islamic thought. He is the national poet of Pakistan.

books.title: The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam

thinkers.start: The Reconstruction of Religious Thought in Islam
